source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex
finding: Core claim: the brain needs two learners. A fast hippocampal system stores single episodes with little overlap. A slow neocortical system learns shared structure by small, interleaved weight changes. The hippocampus replays traces to cortex off-line (rest, slow-wave sleep) so cortex gets interleaved training.
numbers: Theory paper with simulations; 39 pages; no single N.
quote: Interleaved learning allows new knowledge to be gradually incorporated into a structured system
limits: Hippocampus was not simulated. It was treated as a source of training data for cortical networks. Reinstatement during sleep is assumed, with sharp waves as supporting evidence only.
agent_relevance: Design rule for the agent: a fast store for new lessons (episodes) and a slow store for general rules, with lessons moved to the rule store only by mixing with old cases.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex - McCloskey and Cohen AB-AC simulation
finding: Replicated McCloskey and Cohen (1989) AB-AC list learning in a back-prop net. After training on the new AC list, recall of the old AB list was almost wiped out before AC performance rose above 0% correct. Humans (Barnes and Underwood 1959) show mild, gradual loss and keep over 50% AB recall after AC reaches asymptote.
numbers: Model axis 0-50 AC trials; humans 1-20 AC trials. Exact curves only in Fig 10.
quote: The pattern McCloskey and Cohen termed catastrophic interference is evident
limits: Model uses arbitrary pairs and a list-context input. The paper itself notes reducing overlap (French 1991) avoids the catastrophe but kills generalisation.
agent_relevance: Baseline fact: sequentially training on a new lesson can erase old ones almost fully. Test every new lesson against old problems before accepting it.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex - penguin simulation (focused vs interleaved)
finding: Rumelhart (1990) semantic net trained 500 epochs on a base corpus of plant and animal facts, then taught that penguins are birds that can swim but not fly. Focused learning (penguin facts only) learned the new fact faster but made the net treat all animals as swimming, non-flying things; birds were hurt a lot. Interleaving the penguin facts with the full corpus gave very little interference, but progress per exposure was slower.
numbers: 100 presentations of penguin-can-swim-move-grow shown; error = summed absolute output error; interference averaged over 15 'can' cases; same learning rate in both conditions. Values only in Fig 11.
quote: with focused learning, the network learns the material about penguins much more rapidly
limits: Small hand-built net; result is qualitative in the text. Fish performance even improved slightly under focused learning because penguin and fish share outputs.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the agent memory test: a new lesson that conflicts with old knowledge should be mixed with old examples, not applied alone. Learning speed and safety trade off.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex - why interleaving is needed (small learning rate, gradient-following)
finding: Cortical learning works by small weight changes that follow the gradient of error over the whole set of experiences. Large updates from one case distort what the net knows about others. A small learning rate means a large effective sample, so structure is found only by slow, interleaved exposure.
numbers: Qualitative argument and equations; cortical learning rate 0.03 in the monkey fit.
limits: Argued for back-prop style distributed nets; authors say it should hold for other gradient-following learners but do not test it.
agent_relevance: Rules should change slowly and only on evidence from many cases; a single case may sit in the episode store.

source: Kim and Fanselow (1992) Modality-specific retrograde amnesia of fear (read through McClelland 1995)
finding: Rats got tone-shock pairs in a context, then hippocampal lesions at different delays. Lesion 1 day after learning left almost no fear. Fear grew steadily the later the lesion, over a 28-day window. Sham rats showed no reliable delay effect.
numbers: Lesion delays 1 to 28 days; freezing measured 7 days after surgery; group sizes not given in the CLS paper.
limits: Seen only through McClelland et al.; original not opened. Fear memory may differ from declarative memory.
agent_relevance: Supports time-graded dependence of new memories on the fast store.

source: Winocur (1990) and Zola-Morgan and Squire (1990) (read through McClelland 1995)
finding: Winocur (rats, social food preference): lesions within 24 h gave chance performance; later lesions gave much better performance. Zola-Morgan and Squire (monkeys): 100 binary object discriminations in five sets of 20, learned about 1, 3, 7, 11, 15 weeks before surgery. Controls fell from about 80% (1-3 weeks) to about 70% (11-15 weeks). Lesioned monkeys were in the low 60s at 1 week and peaked near 70% at 11 weeks.
numbers: Monkeys: 11 lesioned, 7 sham; tested on all 100 items over two 50-trial sessions two weeks after surgery; 14 trials per pair.
limits: McClelland et al. call the monkey evidence for consolidation weak and noisy (the 11-week point is anomalous). Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: A gradual rise of lesioned performance with training-lesion delay is the signature of consolidation, but it is small here.

source: Squire and Cohen (1979) ECT patients and TV shows (read through McClelland 1995)
finding: Depressed patients given electroconvulsive treatment recalled details of TV shows from different years before treatment. Loss was graded: shows from the years just before treatment were hit most, older ones spared. Used as human support for years-long consolidation.
numbers: Time axis up to about 3000 days.
limits: Authors say depression before treatment may have affected initial storage and ECT affects more than the hippocampus; the weakest of the four data sets.
agent_relevance: Graded retrograde loss means the fast store matters most for recent items.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex - quantitative two-memory model and fitted parameters
finding: Simple two-compartment model: hippocampal trace strength decays exponentially (rate D_h); off-line reinstatement happens at a rate r times residual strength; cortex learns at rate C and decays at D_c. Fitted to four consolidation studies.
numbers: Table 1 hippocampal decay D_h per day: Winocur 0.250, Kim and Fanselow 0.050, Zola-Morgan and Squire 0.035, Squire and Cohen 0.001. Monkey network: learning rate 0.03, hippocampal decay 0.025/day (down to one sixth in 10 weeks), reinstatement 0.1 per trial per day, so about 1.5 times a day when fresh and 0.15 at 10 weeks.
limits: Five free parameters per study and only four data sets. The paper says the frequency and timing of reinstatement are completely unknown. Other parameter sets also fit.
agent_relevance: Replay frequency should fall as a lesson ages and as the rule store absorbs it. Replays per item can be a budgeted parameter.

source: McClelland, McNaughton and O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems in the hippocampus and neocortex - simulated monkey experiment details
finding: A 16-16-16 net with 100 input-output pairs, background trials and reinstated trials reproduced the small consolidation effect. Probability of retrieving at least one trace: 0.6 at the end of training, 0.47 for items learned just before sham surgery, 0.19 for items 7 weeks before surgery, 0.05 for items 15 weeks before.
numbers: Cortical training trials ranged from 25 (1-week items) to 63 (15-week items); reinstatement probability at test R=0.07.
limits: The model explains why the monkey effect is small: much cortical learning happens during original training and hippocampal traces decay fast.
agent_relevance: Consolidation gains are small when initial exposure is already large; replay does not always add value.

source: Merzenich on focal dystonia (personal communication cited in McClelland 1995)
finding: Reported: highly repetitive sensory-motor practice (focused learning) reduced the diversity of responses of neurons in sensory cortex and caused focal dystonia. Interleaved practice on a battery of exercises corrected the syndrome in monkeys and humans.
numbers: No numbers given.
limits: Personal communication, not peer reviewed in this paper.
agent_relevance: Anecdotal support for harm from narrow repeated practice.

source: Shin, Lee, Kim and Kim (2017) Continual Learning with Deep Generative Replay
finding: First explicit CLS-inspired deep net: a generator (hippocampus-like) makes pseudo-samples of past tasks and a solver learns new data mixed with them. No old data stored. Replaying random noise with old labels did not help; replaying generated realistic samples did.
numbers: MNIST solver chain over 5 generations, each trained only from the previous scholar: 98.81, 98.64, 98.58, 98.53, 98.56 percent. Permuted MNIST: near full accuracy on all tasks with replay vs catastrophic forgetting for plain solver.
limits: Small image tasks. Generators degrade on harder data. Not a language model.
agent_relevance: Old tasks can be kept by regenerating them, not storing them. For an LLM agent: generate probe problems from past lessons.

source: Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks (EWC)
finding: EWC slows learning on weights that mattered for old tasks (a synaptic consolidation view), not replay. On permuted MNIST only EWC kept old tasks while learning new ones; L2 kept old tasks but could not learn the new one; plain SGD forgot.
numbers: Permuted MNIST over many tasks; dropout-SGD held only about 2 permutations reasonably. Atari: 10 games in sequence from a pool of 19.
limits: Later work (van de Ven 2019) shows EWC fails in class-incremental settings without task identity.
agent_relevance: Weight protection is a competing route to replay; a scaffold-only agent has no weights to protect, so tests on old cases are the analog.

source: van de Ven and Tolias (2019) Three scenarios for continual learning
finding: Compared methods in task-, domain- and class-incremental settings, 20 seeds. Regularisation (EWC, SI) works only when task identity is given. In class-incremental learning only replay worked.
numbers: Split MNIST Class-IL: none 19.90, EWC 20.01, Online EWC 19.96, SI 19.99, LwF 23.85, DGR 90.79, DGR+distill 91.79, iCaRL (2000 exemplars) 94.57, offline 97.94. Domain-IL: none 59.21, EWC 63.95, DGR 95.72, DGR+distill 96.83. Permuted MNIST Class-IL: EWC 25.04, Online EWC 33.88, DGR 92.19, DGR+distill 96.38.
quote: only methods using replay obtained good performance
limits: MNIST only. Authors warn generative replay may not scale to harder data; replaying current-task inputs (LwF) still beat regularisation.
agent_relevance: When the agent must pick the right rule without being told the problem type, replay of old cases is what held up.

source: Buzzega et al. (2020) Dark Experience for General Continual Learning (DER)
finding: A plain experience-replay buffer (interleave old with new) beat many specialised methods. Adding logit matching on replayed samples (DER, DER++) helped more.
numbers: Seq-CIFAR-10 Class-IL (buffer 200): SGD 19.62, oEWC 19.49, SI 19.48, ER 44.79, iCaRL 49.02, GEM 25.54, A-GEM 20.04, FDR 30.91, joint 92.20. MNIST-360 buffer 200: ER 49.27, MER 48.58, GSS 43.92, DER 55.22, DER++ 54.16; buffer 1000: ER 75.18, DER 75.97.
quote: a simple Experience Replay baseline consistently outperforms cutting-edge methods
limits: Image classification; DER vs ER gaps are small on some benchmarks and depend on buffer size.
agent_relevance: Simple interleaving of stored old cases is a strong baseline. Test any complex consolidation against it.

source: Kemker and Kanan (2018) FearNet: Brain-Inspired Model for Incremental Learning
finding: Explicit CLS model: a fast hippocampal-like store (HC, kept exemplars), a slow mPFC network trained during simulated sleep by pseudo-rehearsal from a generative autoencoder, plus a basolateral-amygdala-like gate that picks which store answers.
numbers: Mean 'all' accuracy normalised to offline MLP: FearNet 0.923 vs iCaRL 0.782, GeppNet 0.759, FEL 0.572, 1-NN 0.729. CIFAR-100 all 0.947 vs iCaRL 0.749; CUB-200 0.891 vs 0.864; AudioSet 0.932 vs 0.733. Offline MLP accuracy 69.9, 59.8, 45.8 percent. With oracle store choice, CIFAR-100 new-class accuracy 0.912 vs 0.824 with the gate. Sleep every 10 sessions; sleeping less often hurt.
limits: Uses pre-extracted ResNet-50 embeddings, not raw pixels. Gate errors lose new-class accuracy. HC keeps recent data until sleep.
agent_relevance: Closest AI copy of the CLS split. A router that decides which store to trust cost accuracy on new items, so routing is a weak link in an agent too.

source: Arani, Sarfraz and Zonooz (2022) Learning Fast, Learning Slow (CLS-ER)
finding: Dual-memory experience replay: a working model plus two exponential-moving-average copies, a fast plastic model and a slow stable model; the stable model is used for inference. Beat DER++ across benchmarks, most when memory is small and task sequences long.
numbers: MNIST-360 buffer 200: CLS-ER 66.37 vs DER++ 54.16, ER 49.27; buffer 500: 75.70 vs 69.62; buffer 1000: 79.54 vs 76.03. S-Tiny-ImageNet buffer 200: +176% relative over ER and +114% over DER++. Components on P-MNIST (buffer 500): stable 75.22, plastic 71.32, working 63.09.
limits: Gains vanish at large buffers (S-Tiny-ImageNet buffer 5120: about 95.7 for all three components). Hyperparameters grid-searched on a small validation set.
agent_relevance: A slow consolidated store beat the fast one on old items, and both were useful. Analogue: a slow rules memory beside a fast recent-lessons memory.

source: Hayes et al. (2021) Replay in Deep Learning: Current Approaches and Missing Biological Elements
finding: Review of replay in ML vs brain. CLS-inspired AI mostly uses generative replay of past inputs; few models have hippocampus-to-cortex feedback in both directions; ML lacks explicit wake and sleep states; the cortex can replay by itself (self-generated replay) while ML replay usually interleaves from a hippocampus-like buffer.
numbers: Review, no new data.
limits: Authors say CLS is probably not the only memory model: procedural memories can be consolidated without the hippocampus.
agent_relevance: Open design gaps: a cheap sleep phase, and self-generated replay by the model itself without stored data.

source: Scialom, Chakrabarty and Muresan (2022) Fine-tuned Language Models are Continual Learners
finding: On T0 (an instruction-tuned LM), learning new generation tasks with 0% rehearsal caused catastrophic loss of T0 zero-shot ability. Rehearsal of only 0.25% of previous data gave almost perfect stability; 1% held performance stationary. New-task results did not depend on the rehearsal level. Final model CT0 learned 8 new tasks across 70 datasets.
numbers: Rehearsal r in {0, 0.25%, 1%}; 100,000 examples per T0 training task so 1% = 1,000 examples; new tasks Simplification, Headline with keyword, Haiku.
quote: at 0% rehearsal, the model catastrophically forgets the T0 zero-shot tasks
limits: Rehearsal uses real stored data. Results shown as relative-gain curves (Figure 1), not tabulated in the text.
agent_relevance: LLM-scale evidence that a tiny replay share (0.25 to 1%) is enough to stop catastrophic forgetting. A few old test cases go a long way.

source: Luo et al. (2025) An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs During Continual Fine-tuning
finding: Forgetting appears in LLMs from 1b to 7b during continual instruction tuning, across domain knowledge, reasoning and reading comprehension. Forgetting got worse as scale grew in this range. Decoder-only BLOOMZ forgot less than encoder-decoder mT0. General instruction tuning first (ALPACA vs LLAMA) reduced later forgetting.
numbers: Models BLOOMZ 1b to 7b, mT0, LLAMA, ALPACA; MMLU 5-shot among the tests.
limits: Authors say the scale effect may come from larger models starting higher, so more to lose. Only up to 7b. I read abstract, intro and setup, not every table.
agent_relevance: Do not assume bigger models are safe from forgetting; the measured trend went the other way.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in LLMs with Self-Synthesized Rehearsal (SSR)
finding: When old training data is unavailable, the model generates inputs from few-shot demos, the latest model refines outputs, and diverse instances are kept for rehearsal. Matches or beats rehearsal on real data while using only 1% real data as seed.
numbers: Llama-2-7b on 10 SuperNI tasks, final average result (AR): non-rehearsal 17.33, RandSel 1% 60.64, RandSel 10% 61.49, SSR 63.23, multitask upper bound 64.69. Alpaca-7b plus 5 tasks: SSR kept general ability better than rehearsal baselines (MMLU 36.9 for one SSR row vs 34.1 for RandSel 10%; table partly garbled in text extraction).
limits: Table columns were hard to read in PDF text. AR values reliable; backward-transfer values not recorded. Small task set (SuperNI).
agent_relevance: Self-generated replay (the model recalls its own old problems) works at 7B scale. This fills the gap Hayes names.

source: Ibrahim et al. (2024) Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train Large Language Models
finding: Learning-rate re-warming and re-decaying plus replay of earlier data matched full re-training on all data. Even 1% replay cut forgetting. 50% replay hurt adaptation to the new data.
numbers: 405M models, hundreds of billions of tokens; weak shift Pile to SlimPajama, strong shift English to German; chosen replay 5% (weak) and 25% (strong); confirmed at 10B scale. 50% replay saw 150B fewer new tokens (SlimPajama) and 100B fewer (German) yet matched the baseline final average loss.
quote: replaying previous data (as little as 1%) is sufficient to mitigate forgetting to a large extent
limits: Replay was of same-source pretraining data; two dataset pairs only; downstream effect of 1, 5, 10% replay was small versus 0%.
agent_relevance: Dose-response: small replay shares work, too much slows learning. Tune the share of old problems mixed into each update.

source: Biderman et al. (2024) LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
finding: Low-rank adapters learn less than full fine-tuning but forget less of the base model's abilities; LoRA mitigates forgetting more than weight decay or dropout. Full fine-tuning learns perturbations of rank 10 to 100 times higher than typical LoRA settings.
numbers: Programming and maths targets; 100K instruction pairs and 20B tokens of continued pretraining.
limits: Abstract-level numbers only recorded.
agent_relevance: Matches the CLS stability-plasticity trade-off: a slower, smaller update protects old skills at a cost to new learning.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Continual Learning via Sparse Memory Finetuning
finding: Updating only the memory slots most activated by new facts relative to pretraining usage (TF-IDF ranking) cut interference. Authors state that replay helps but does not scale as experience grows.
numbers: NaturalQuestions F1 dropped 89% after full finetuning on new TriviaQA facts, 71% with LoRA, 11% with sparse memory finetuning, at the same level of new-knowledge learning.
limits: Needs a memory-layer architecture; two QA tasks; no replay baseline in the headline result.
agent_relevance: Sparse, separate storage of new facts (a pattern-separation idea) protects old knowledge, as CLS predicts.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG
finding: Uses hippocampal indexing theory (not the CLS replay argument): the LLM extracts a knowledge graph (pattern separation) and Personalized PageRank retrieves by pattern completion. Improves multi-hop QA over retrieval baselines.
numbers: Up to 20% better than prior RAG on multi-hop QA; R@2 +11 and R@5 +20 on 2WikiMultiHopQA; single-step retrieval comparable or better than IRCoT while 10-20 times cheaper and 6-13 times faster.
limits: Retrieval, not weight consolidation; a loose link to CLS.
agent_relevance: Memory-as-index design: store new lessons as linked facts and retrieve by association rather than overwrite.

source: Qi et al. (2024) Interactive Continual Learning: Fast and Slow Thinking
finding: Uses CLS theory to pair a ViT (System 1, fast) with a multimodal LLM (System 2) that handles hard examples found by an outlier detector; the ViT memory is updated. Reported less forgetting than prior methods on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and ImageNet-R.
numbers: Authors report over 3% gain in continual-learning accuracy on ImageNet-R (buffer 600) from adding System 2.
limits: Vision classification; the LLM is a helper, not the thing being consolidated. Claims are the authors' own.
agent_relevance: An LLM can act as the slow, deliberate arbiter on hard cases routed from a fast learner.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis and McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS theory updated
finding: Update of CLS, cited by Hayes, FearNet and van de Ven. Not opened by me. Full text could not be retrieved this session.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Cited only; no claim of content beyond the title.
agent_relevance: Follow up: selective, goal-weighted replay instead of uniform replay.
